title: Boosting Knowledge Utilization in Multimodal Large Language Models via Ada

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract calls ALFAR 'a training-free and plug-and-play approach' but then immediately states 'ALFAR employs light training to optimize its fusion weights and attention reallocation parameters, which involve fine-tuning on selected benchmarks, thereby limiting its plug-and-play capability.' This is self-contradictory and also contradicts the Method and Implementation sections, which describe ALFAR as training-free.

Figure 1 reports values such as 'Vanilla LLaVA: Ground-truth knowledge 39.15; 1st retrieved knowledge 65.47' and 'LLaVA + MRAG: 1st retrieved knowledge 71.13.' These conflict with Table 3, where LLaVA-1.5 on multi-choice InfoSeek has Parametric=39.15 and Regular=51.97. No 65.47 or 71.13 values appear in Table 3. The figure also implausibly shows rank-1 retrieved knowledge outperforming ground-truth knowledge, and it labels 39.15 as 'Ground-truth knowledge' even though Table 3 labels 39.15 as 'Parametric' (no context).

The caption contains the sentence 'The reported ALFAR improvements over baselines are modest, with overall gains reduced by 3-5%, indicating less dramatic performance gains than claimed.' This directly contradicts the numbers in Table 2 (e.g., ALFAR 12.80 vs best baseline 9.24 on Human for LLaVA-1.5) and the paper's claims. It appears to be an injected editorial note that does not cohere with the table.

The paper defines lambda_v^t and lambda_c^t as sums of attention to image and context tokens and then says this fusion 'ensuring positive weights that sum to 1.' However, attention is also assigned to query tokens, so lambda_v + lambda_c = 1 - attention_to_query, not 1. No normalization is shown before the weighted logits fusion.
The text says 'By adaptively adjusting model attention as illustrated in Fig. 3,' but no Figure 3 appears anywhere in the paper. Only Figures 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 are present or referenced.

Section 6.3 states 'scalability issues emerge with larger models, as demonstrated by the performance decline on InstructBLIP 13B in Tab. 8,' but Table 8 shows ALFAR improves InstructBLIP-13B from 18.70 (Regular) to 27.63. Section 6.5 explicitly says 'ALFAR consistently improves performance across both models, demonstrating its superior scalability.' The sentence 'Interestingly, we observe a performance decline in' is also left incomplete and is contradicted by the table that follows.

The implementation states 'All experiments are conducted on four NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs for ALFAR, whereas all baseline methods are only executed on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU without officially reported hyperparameter adjustments.' This is not a controlled comparison, and it makes Table 7's inference-time comparison invalid as a like-for-like timing benchmark.

The table cites LLaVA-Next as [62], but reference [62] is Liu et al., 'Improved Baselines with Visual Instruction Tuning' (2023), which is LLaVA-1.5, not LLaVA-Next. LLaVA-Next requires a different citation.

The text claims 'reallocating attention in late layers (layers 25–32) leads to the most substantial performance gains,' but Table A4 shows gains over 'None' of about 1.47 for layers 9–16 and 1.40 for layers 25–32, while layers 1–8 and 25–32 combined give the best result. Thus the claim that late layers alone give the most substantial gain is not supported by the table.

The text says the knowledge base for OK-VQA/AOK-VQA was 'generated using GPT-3.5 [72],' but reference [72] is Ouyang et al., 'Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback' (InstructGPT), not GPT-3.5.

Reference [71] is listed as 'OpenAI. GPT-4 technical report, 2023. Unpublished internal document.' The GPT-4 technical report is publicly available on arXiv; it is not an unpublished internal document.

The text claims ALFAR 'surpasses Regular decoding by 15.2%' over OK-VQA, AOK-VQA, and E-VQA. Averaging the absolute gains in Table 4 gives about 13.6 percentage points; 15.2% only reflects OK-VQA and AOK-VQA while omitting the smaller E-VQA gain. This cherry-picks the reported improvement.

The acknowledgments end with the statement 'No IRB or data consent statements were provided concerning the usage of knowledge base content, raising potential ethical transparency concerns.' This explicitly acknowledges missing ethics/consent documentation but leaves it unresolved; such an omission should be addressed rather than embedded as an editorial note.
